1(a).assumed: Coherent waves have a constant phase difference.

1(b)(i).assumed: Path difference is the difference between the two distances from the sources.

1(b)(ii).assumed: At a minimum the waves arrive in antiphase: π radians.

1(b)(iii).assumed: First minimum has path difference λ/2.

1(c)(i).assumed: Period = divisions per cycle × time-base; frequency = 1/period.

1(c)(ii).assumed: v = fλ with kHz converted to Hz.

2(a)(i).assumed: Area under a force–extension graph is work done, stored as elastic energy.

2(a)(ii).assumed: Estimate area under a curve by counting squares × energy per square.

2(a)(iii).assumed: Rubber shows hysteresis; the difference between loading and unloading work is dissipated as heat.

2(b)(ii).assumed: Strain = stress/Young modulus, with GPa converted; strain has no unit.

2(c).assumed: Doubling diameter quadruples area, quartering extension and hence energy ½Fx at the same load.

3(a).assumed: Momentum conserved in all collisions; elastic means KE conserved, inelastic means KE lost; calculate both before and after.

3(b).assumed: Impulse = area under the F–t triangle = change in momentum; v = impulse/m from rest.

4(a)(ii).assumed: Volume = area × height; mass = ρV; weight = mg.

4(b).assumed: A floating body displaces its own weight of water; depth = displaced volume ÷ cross-sectional area.

4(c).assumed: Same weight of less dense liquid must be displaced, so a larger volume and greater depth (depth ∝ 1/ρ).

5(a).assumed: Kirchhoff's second law: e.m.f. = p.d. across load + p.d. across internal resistance (Ir).

5(b).assumed: Compare V = −rI + E with y = mx + c: intercept is E, gradient is −r.

5(c)(i).assumed: Read V at the current from the graph; R = V/I with mA in A.

5(c)(ii).assumed: P = VI; energy = Pt with minutes in seconds.

6.assumed: LDR resistance falls in light; potential divider output across fixed resistor; choose values with the divider equation; variable resistor adjusts threshold.

7(a)(i).assumed: Gradient from a large triangle, with powers of ten handled.

7(a)(ii).assumed: Rearrange the given gradient = hc/e for h, using data-sheet constants.

7(a)(iii).assumed: Worst line is steepest or shallowest through all error bars.

7(a)(iv).assumed: Percentage uncertainty = difference between best and worst gradients ÷ best × 100.

7(b)(i).assumed: Photon energy hc/λ (nm to m); φ eV to J; KEmax = E − φ.

7(b)(ii).assumed: Photon energy depends only on wavelength; intensity changes number of photons, so KEmax is unchanged.
